Content:
Suppose that [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are sets, and [MATH: U] is a universal set.

Content:
De Morgan's law for intersections states that the complement of the intersection of [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] is the union of their complements. Symbolically, we can express this as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \overline{A \cap B} = \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}]

Content:
We can get an intuitive understanding of De Morgan's law for intersections using the diagram shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2e07e75a48f3587948e5fa502cc0d105]

Content:
The shaded region corresponds to [MATH: \overline{A} \cup \overline{B},] and the non-shaded region corresponds to [MATH: A \cap B.] It's clear from the diagram that by taking the complement of the non-shaded region, we get the shaded region.

Content:
Although this diagram helps to build intuition, it does not constitute a formal mathematical proof. We usually resort to one of the following methods to formally prove De Morgan's laws.

Content:
1. Using truth tables.
2. Using the property that for sets [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y,] we have [MATH: X = Y] if and only if [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are subsets of each other. In this case, we'd need to prove the following:
[MATH: \overline{A \cap B} \subseteq \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad\overline{A} \cup \overline{B} \subseteq \overline{A \cap B}]
3. Establishing a chain of equivalent statements shows that membership of the first set is equivalent to membership of the second set. In this case, we'd need to show that for all [MATH: x\in U,] we have
[MATH: x\in \overline{A \cap B} \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x\in \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}.]

Content:
We'll focus on the second and third methods in this topic.

Content:
Before we discuss our first proof, it may be no surprise that De Morgan's law for conjunctions is very useful in these proofs. Recall that if [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] are statements, then De Morgan's law for conjunctions states:
[MATH: \lnot (P\land Q) \equiv \lnot P \lor \lnot Q]
De Morgan's law for intersections is the set-theoretic equivalent of De Morgan's law for conjunctions, and the latter is often used to prove the former.

Content:
Let's prove the following subset relation:
[MATH: \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}\subseteq \overline{A \cap B}]

Content:
To do this, we must demonstrate that a fixed but arbitrary element of the first set is also an element of the second set.

Content:
So, we start by considering an arbitrary element of [MATH: \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}] and use the definition of the union of sets.

Content:
> [MATH: x \in \overline{A} \cup \overline{B} \quad\Rightarrow\quad ( x \in \overline{A} ) \lor ( x \in \overline{B} )]

Content:
The idea is to manipulate the statement on the right-hand side so that we can apply De Morgan's law for conjunctions.

Content:
[MATH: \lnot P \lor \lnot Q \equiv \lnot (P\land Q)]

Content:
Notice that the statements [MATH: ( x \in \overline{A} ) \lor ( x \in \overline{B} )] and [MATH: \lnot P \lor \lnot Q] already look quite similar:

Content:
So, our next step is to use the definition of the set complement.

Content:
> [MATH: ( x \in \overline{A} ) \lor ( x \in \overline{B} ) \quad\Rightarrow\quad ( x \notin A ) \lor ( x \notin B )]

Content:
Then, we apply the definition of negation.

Content:
> [MATH: ( x \notin A ) \lor ( x \notin B ) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \lnot ( x \in A ) \lor \lnot ( x \in B )]

Content:
Then, we use De Morgan's law for conjunctions.

Content:
> [MATH: \lnot ( x \in A ) \lor \lnot ( x \in B ) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \lnot \big( (x \in A) \land (x \in B) \big)]

Content:
The hard part of the proof is done at this point. We just need to rewrite this statement using set-theoretic definitions.

Content:
First, we apply the definition of intersection.

Content:
> [MATH: \lnot \big( (x \in A) \land (x \in B) \big) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \lnot ( x \in A \cap B )]

Content:
Then, we use the definition of negation once more.

Content:
> [MATH: \lnot ( x \in A \cap B ) \quad\Rightarrow\quad x \notin A \cap B]

Content:
Finally, we apply the definition of the set complement once more.

Content:
> [MATH: x \notin A \cap B \quad\Rightarrow\quad x \in \overline{A \cap B}]

Content:
So, we have shown that [MATH: x\in \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}] implies [MATH: x\in \overline{A \cap B}.] Our proof is complete, and we now state our conclusion.

Content:
> So, if [MATH: x \in\overline{A} \cup \overline{B},] then [MATH: x \in \overline{A \cap B}.] By the definition of a subset, this means
> [MATH: \overline{A} \cup \overline{B} \subseteq \overline{A \cap B}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are sets, and [MATH: U] is a universal set.

Content:
De Morgan's law for intersections states that the complement of the intersection of [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] is the union of their complements. Symbolically, we can express this as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \overline{A \cap B} = \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}]

Content:
We can get an intuitive understanding of De Morgan's law for intersections using the diagram shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2e07e75a48f3587948e5fa502cc0d105]

Content:
The shaded region corresponds to [MATH: \overline{A} \cup \overline{B},] and the non-shaded region corresponds to [MATH: A \cap B.] It's clear from the diagram that by taking the complement of the non-shaded region, we get the shaded region.

Content:
Although this diagram helps to build intuition, it does not constitute a formal mathematical proof. We usually resort to one of the following methods to formally prove De Morgan's laws.

Content:
1. Using truth tables.
2. Using the property that for sets [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y,] we have [MATH: X = Y] if and only if [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are subsets of each other. In this case, we'd need to prove the following:
[MATH: \overline{A \cap B} \subseteq \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad\overline{A} \cup \overline{B} \subseteq \overline{A \cap B}]
3. Establishing a chain of equivalent statements shows that membership of the first set is equivalent to membership of the second set. In this case, we'd need to show that for all [MATH: x\in U,] we have
[MATH: x\in \overline{A \cap B} \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x\in \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}.]

Content:
We'll focus on the second and third methods in this topic.

Content:
Before we discuss our first proof, it may be no surprise that De Morgan's law for conjunctions is very useful in these proofs. Recall that if [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] are statements, then De Morgan's law for conjunctions states:
[MATH: \lnot (P\land Q) \equiv \lnot P \lor \lnot Q]
De Morgan's law for intersections is the set-theoretic equivalent of De Morgan's law for conjunctions, and the latter is often used to prove the former.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Proving a Subset Relation

Content:
Let's prove the following subset relation:
[MATH: \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}\subseteq \overline{A \cap B}]

Content:
To do this, we must demonstrate that a fixed but arbitrary element of the first set is also an element of the second set.

Content:
So, we start by considering an arbitrary element of [MATH: \overline{A} \cup \overline{B}] and use the definition of the union of sets.

Content:
> [MATH: x \in \overline{A} \cup \overline{B} \quad\Rightarrow\quad ( x \in \overline{A} ) \lor ( x \in \overline{B} )]

Content:
The idea is to manipulate the statement on the right-hand side so that we can apply De Morgan's law for conjunctions.

Content:
[MATH: \lnot P \lor \lnot Q \equiv \lnot (P\land Q)]

Content:
Notice that the statements [MATH: ( x \in \overline{A} ) \lor ( x \in \overline{B} )] and [MATH: \lnot P \lor \lnot Q] already look quite similar:

Content:
So, our next step is to use the definition of the set complement.

Content:
> [MATH: ( x \in \overline{A} ) \lor ( x \in \overline{B} ) \quad\Rightarrow\quad ( x \notin A ) \lor ( x \notin B )]

Content:
Then, we apply the definition of negation.

Content:
> [MATH: ( x \notin A ) \lor ( x \notin B ) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \lnot ( x \in A ) \lor \lnot ( x \in B )]

Content:
Then, we use De Morgan's law for conjunctions.

Content:
> [MATH: \lnot ( x \in A ) \lor \lnot ( x \in B ) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \lnot \big( (x \in A) \land (x \in B) \big)]

Content:
The hard part of the proof is done at this point. We just need to rewrite this statement using set-theoretic definitions.

Content:
First, we apply the definition of intersection.

Content:
> [MATH: \lnot \big( (x \in A) \land (x \in B) \big) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \lnot ( x \in A \cap B )]

Content:
Then, we use the definition of negation once more.

Content:
> [MATH: \lnot ( x \in A \cap B ) \quad\Rightarrow\quad x \notin A \cap B]

Content:
Finally, we apply the definition of the set complement once more.

Content:
> [MATH: x \notin A \cap B \quad\Rightarrow\quad x \in \overline{A \cap B}]

Content:
